lessons.title: Commodity Cyclicals: Metals, Cement, and Chemicals

body.text: Commodity companies do not control their selling price, so their profit is a spread: the gap between what the market pays for their product and what they pay for inputs. Track the spread and the supply cycle, not the revenue line.

children.text: Metals, cement, and commodity chemicals sit at the deep end of the cyclical spectrum, but they are not identical. Steel prices are set in a global market dominated by China. Cement prices are set region by region inside India. Chemicals range from pure commodities to specialty products with some pricing power. This lesson shows what actually drives earnings in each, and which numbers to watch.

children.text: The Supply Cycle: Why Booms Create Their Own Busts

Demand swings get the headlines, but in commodities the supply side often matters more. A new steel plant or cement line takes years to plan and build. Companies decide to build when prices and profits are high, and the new capacity arrives years later, often just as demand cools. The result is a cycle that repeats with remarkable regularity.

events.title: Tight supply, high prices
events.description: Demand runs ahead of capacity. Prices and EBITDA per tonne hit records. Stocks rally and every company reports its best-ever quarter.

events.title: Capex announcements
events.description: Flush with cash, companies across the industry announce expansions, often funded partly by debt. Management commentary is confident.

events.title: New capacity arrives
events.description: Two to four years later, plants commission together. Supply jumps just as demand growth slows. Utilisation falls and prices soften.

events.title: Oversupply and losses
events.description: Prices fall towards the cash cost of the weaker producers. High-cost and highly indebted companies post losses. Capex plans are cancelled.

events.title: Closures and consolidation
events.description: Weak players shut plants, sell out, or go through insolvency. No new capacity is built. As demand recovers, supply tightens and the cycle restarts.

body.text: A useful rule: when every company in a commodity industry is announcing big expansions at the same time, the best part of the cycle is usually already priced in. When nobody wants to build and weak players are closing, the next upcycle is often being set up.

children.text: Metals: Spreads, China, and the Cost Curve

markDefs.definition: Operating profit before depreciation, interest, and tax, divided by tonnes sold. It shows how much a metal or cement company earns on each unit and is the most comparable profitability measure across the industry.

children.text: every quarter, and it is the number that moves the stock. It is essentially a spread: steel selling price minus iron ore, coking coal, and conversion costs. Because China produces more than half the world's steel, a slowdown in Chinese property construction can push Chinese mills to export more, pulling down prices everywhere, including in India. Indian steel stocks often react to Chinese data before any change shows up in domestic demand.

cells: Iron ore and other raw materials

body.caption: At 2 crore tonnes (20 million tonnes) sold, ₹11,000 per tonne = ₹22,000 crore of EBITDA; ₹5,500 per tonne = ₹11,000 crore

body.title: Rebuild the Spread
body.prompt: Starting from the good year in the table, steel realisation rises 5% to ₹57,750 per tonne, but coking coal cost jumps 25% to ₹25,000 per tonne. Other costs are unchanged. What is the new EBITDA per tonne in rupees?
body.explanation: 57,750 - 25,000 - 12,000 - 12,000 = ₹8,750 per tonne. Steel prices went up, yet profit per tonne fell about 20% from ₹11,000. This is why you track the spread, not the selling price. Rising revenue at a metal company is not good news if input costs are rising faster.

markDefs.definition: A ranking of all producers in an industry from lowest to highest cost of production. In a downturn, prices tend to fall until the highest-cost producers can no longer cover their cash costs.

children.text: The second concept that matters in metals is the

. In a bust, prices tend to fall until enough high-cost producers are losing cash and cut output. A company near the bottom of the global cost curve keeps earning money when others are losing it. Hindustan Zinc, with its own mines, is often cited as one of the lower-cost zinc producers globally. Companies with captive iron ore mines have a similar advantage in steel. Low cost does not remove cyclicality, but it decides who survives the trough intact.

body.title: Who Survives the Trough?
body.question: Global aluminium prices fall to a level where the average producer is just breaking even at the cash level. Which Indian producer is best placed?
options: A producer that buys alumina from the market and grid power at commercial rates
An integrated producer with captive bauxite mines, its own alumina refinery, and captive power plants
A producer that has just completed a large debt-funded expansion
All producers are equally affected, because they all sell at the same global price
body.explanation: Everyone receives the same global price, but costs differ widely. Captive bauxite, alumina, and power put an integrated producer lower on the cost curve, so it still earns a margin when the average producer is breaking even. The debt-funded producer also carries higher interest, making its position the worst.

children.text: Cement is heavy and cheap relative to its weight, so moving it more than a few hundred kilometres by road eats into margins quickly. That makes cement a regional business. Prices in the South can fall because of new capacity there while prices in the North hold firm. Imports are rarely a threat. Demand is tied to Indian housing and infrastructure rather than China, and it is seasonal: the July to September monsoon quarter is typically the weakest of the year, as construction slows.

The industry has also been consolidating. The Adani group's 2022 acquisition of Ambuja Cements and ACC from Holcim, and UltraTech's continued acquisitions, have concentrated capacity among fewer, larger players. Consolidation tends to make pricing more disciplined, which pushes cement slightly towards the less-deep end of the cyclical range. It does not make cement defensive: new capacity additions and energy cost spikes still squeeze EBITDA per tonne hard.

body.title: Why Cement Is Different
body.textWithBlank: Because cement is expensive to transport over long distances, cement prices in India are set largely at a ___ level rather than globally.
body.explanation: High freight cost relative to product value keeps cement markets regional. That is why a cement company's regional exposure, and new capacity coming up in its specific region, matter as much as national demand.

Multi-year contracts and customer approval processes create switching costs
Margins more stable, but volumes still follow customer inventory cycles
Cyclical, but closer to the middle of the spectrum

children.text: Indian chemicals investors learnt the limits of the specialty label after the pandemic boom. Many companies traded at premium valuations on the China plus one story in 2021 and 2022. Then global customers ran down their inventories, Chinese supply returned at low prices, and earnings at a large number of Indian chemical companies fell in FY24. The businesses were not broken, but their earnings proved far more cyclical than their valuations had assumed.

body.title: Record Quarter, Record Risk?
body.scenario: Aman, a salaried investor, reads that a steel company has just posted its highest-ever quarterly EBITDA per tonne. Steel prices are near multi-year highs. The company and three of its listed peers have each announced capacity expansions of 30% or more over the next three years. The stock trades at a P/E of 7, well below the Nifty 50. Aman thinks it looks like a cheap, fast-growing company.
body.prompt: What is Aman missing? What would you check before buying?
body.modelAnswer: Aman is looking at peak-cycle signals and reading them as a growth story. Record spreads, near-peak prices, and industry-wide expansions are Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the supply cycle, which historically lead to oversupply once the new capacity arrives. The low P/E is calculated on peak earnings that may not last, a trap Chapter 4 covers in detail. Before buying, check: where EBITDA per tonne sits against its 10-year range; how much total industry capacity is coming online versus expected demand growth; how the expansions are funded, since debt adds financial leverage into a potential downturn; the company's position on the cost curve; and what Chinese steel exports and prices are doing.

cards.definition: The gap between a commodity producer's selling price and its key input costs, which drives profit more than revenue does.
Operating profit before depreciation, interest, and tax, divided by tonnes sold; the core profitability metric for metal and cement companies.
A ranking of producers from lowest to highest cost; low-cost producers stay profitable when prices fall to the level where high-cost ones lose money.
Actual production as a percentage of maximum possible production; high utilisation supports pricing, low utilisation signals oversupply.
The London Metal Exchange, whose prices serve as global benchmarks for aluminium, zinc, copper, and other base metals.

body.label: London Metal Exchange (LME)
body.description: Benchmark prices for aluminium, zinc, copper, and other base metals that drive earnings at Hindalco, Vedanta, and Hindustan Zinc.

points: Commodity companies are price takers; their profit is a spread between selling price and input costs, best tracked as EBITDA per tonne
The supply cycle drives busts: capacity is announced at the peak and arrives years later, often into slowing demand
Metals are the deepest cyclicals, priced globally and heavily influenced by China
Position on the cost curve decides which producers stay profitable in a trough
Cement is a regional, domestic cyclical, softened somewhat by consolidation but still exposed to capacity additions and energy costs
Specialty chemicals are less cyclical than commodity chemicals but still follow customer inventory cycles and Chinese supply

body.text: The steel spread figures and Aman's scenario are illustrative. Descriptions of listed companies and industry events summarise public information for education and should be checked against the latest filings. This lesson is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
